questions.stem: How are the terms of trade calculated?
options: (Index of export prices / Index of import prices) x 100
(Index of import prices / Index of export prices) x 100
Export value minus import value
(Export volume / Import volume) x 100
questions.why: Export prices on top. Getting this the wrong way round inverts the whole answer.
whyNot: That inverts the formula.
That is the trade balance.
That is a volume ratio, not the terms of trade.

questions.stem: Export prices index 114, import prices index 105. What are the terms of trade?
questions.why: (114 / 105) x 100 = 108.6, an improvement of 8.6% from a base of 100.
whyNot: That inverts the formula.
That uses an incorrect calculation.
That is the difference in the indices, not the ratio.

questions.stem: Export prices index 106, import prices index 128. What are the terms of trade?
whyNot: That inverts the formula.
That uses an incorrect calculation.
That is the difference in the indices.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an improvement in the terms of trade?
options: Export prices have risen relative to import prices, so exports buy more imports
Export volumes have risen relative to import volumes
The trade balance has moved into surplus
Both export and import prices have fallen
questions.why: The terms of trade are a price ratio, not a volume or value measure.
whyNot: It concerns prices, not volumes.
That is the trade balance, a different measure.
What matters is their movement relative to each other.

questions.stem: The terms of trade move from 108.6 to 82.8. What is the percentage change?
options: A fall of 23.8%
A fall of 25.8%
A rise of 23.8%
A fall of 31.2%
whyNot: That divides by the new figure rather than the old.
The index has fallen, so the change is negative.
That uses an incorrect denominator.

questions.stem: Higher domestic inflation than trading partners has what effect?
options: The terms of trade improve and competitiveness worsens
The terms of trade worsen and competitiveness improves
Both the terms of trade and competitiveness improve
Neither is affected
questions.why: Export prices rise faster than import prices, improving the ratio while making the country less competitive. Almost everything that improves one worsens the other.
whyNot: Higher inflation raises export prices, improving the ratio.
They move in opposite directions.
Relative price movements affect both.

questions.stem: Faster productivity growth than competitors has what effect?
options: The terms of trade deteriorate and competitiveness improves
The terms of trade improve and competitiveness worsens
Both deteriorate
Neither is affected
questions.why: Lower unit costs mean lower export prices, which worsens the price ratio while improving competitiveness.
whyNot: Lower export prices worsen the ratio.
Competitiveness improves with productivity.
Both are affected.

questions.stem: An appreciation of the currency has what immediate effect on the terms of trade?
options: They improve, because export prices rise in foreign currency and import prices fall in domestic currency
They deteriorate, because exports become dearer
They are unaffected, because the exchange rate is not a price
They improve only if the Marshall-Lerner condition holds
questions.why: The price ratio moves favourably immediately, whatever happens to volumes afterwards.
whyNot: Dearer exports raise the export price index, which improves the ratio.
The exchange rate directly changes both price indices.
The condition concerns the trade balance, not the terms of trade.

questions.stem: An improvement in the terms of trade occurs and demand for exports is price elastic. What happens to export revenue?
options: It falls, because the proportional fall in quantity exceeds the proportional rise in price
It rises, because prices are higher
It is unchanged, because the effects offset exactly
It cannot be determined without knowing import elasticity
questions.why: With PED greater than 1, a price rise reduces total revenue.
whyNot: That would be the result with inelastic demand.
Exact offsetting occurs only at unit elasticity.
Export revenue depends on export elasticity alone.

questions.stem: An improvement in the terms of trade occurs and demand for exports is price inelastic. What happens to export revenue?
options: It rises, because quantity falls proportionally less than the price rises
It falls, because quantity falls
It is unchanged
It depends on the exchange rate regime
questions.why: With PED less than 1, a price rise raises total revenue.
whyNot: The quantity fall is proportionally smaller than the price rise.
Revenue changes unless elasticity is exactly 1.
Elasticity determines the outcome.

questions.stem: Why is an improvement in the terms of trade not automatically good news?
options: It usually reflects lost competitiveness, and export volumes and employment may fall
It always causes inflation
It reduces the country's imports of essential goods
It always worsens the balance of payments
questions.why: Real income rises for consumers and export sector workers may lose out, which is a distributional effect worth naming.
whyNot: Higher export prices are not inflationary domestically.
It makes imports cheaper relative to exports.
The effect on the balance depends on elasticities.

questions.stem: What does the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis propose?
options: The terms of trade of primary product exporters decline over the long run relative to manufactures
Primary product prices rise faster than manufactured goods prices
Terms of trade converge between all countries over time
Commodity prices are stable in the long run
questions.why: The reasoning rests on income inelastic demand for primary products and on differing market power in passing on productivity gains.
whyNot: The hypothesis predicts the opposite.
It predicts divergence, not convergence.
Commodity prices are notably volatile.

questions.stem: Why is the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis used as an argument for diversification?
options: A country dependent on primary exports faces a structural decline in its purchasing power
Diversified economies always grow faster
Primary production is always less profitable per unit
Manufacturing requires no capital investment
questions.why: It adds a long-run structural problem on top of the short-run volatility of commodity prices.
whyNot: Growth depends on many factors.
Profitability varies; the argument concerns the trend in relative prices.
Manufacturing is capital-intensive.

questions.stem: Which condition determines whether a price change moves the trade balance in the expected direction?
options: The Marshall-Lerner condition, that the two elasticities sum to more than 1
The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis
Purchasing power parity
The Laffer curve
questions.why: Referring to it in a terms of trade question shows synthesis between topics and earns a mark.
whyNot: That concerns the long-run trend in relative prices.
That concerns long-run exchange rate determination.
That concerns tax revenue.

questions.stem: A country exports tourism services and imports oil. Oil prices rise sharply. What happens?
options: The terms of trade deteriorate and real national income falls without any change in output
The terms of trade improve, because tourism is a service
The terms of trade are unaffected, because oil is not exported
The trade balance necessarily moves into surplus
questions.why: The import price index rises directly while tourism prices adjust slowly because they are set in advance.
whyNot: A higher import price index worsens the ratio.
Import prices are half the ratio.
A higher import bill worsens the balance, other things equal.

questions.stem: Why is a deterioration in the terms of trade particularly damaging for a developing economy?
options: It must export more merely to buy the same quantity of essential imports such as fuel and machinery
It always causes a currency appreciation
It reduces the country's export volumes automatically
It prevents the country from receiving aid
questions.why: Real purchasing power falls even with unchanged output, and the imports affected are often essential capital and consumption goods.
whyNot: It tends to put downward pressure on the currency.
Volumes respond to prices and elasticities rather than automatically.
Aid is unaffected.
